blocks.text: Jeremiah addresses the deported people as a community, not merely as isolated individuals. The commands to build homes, plant gardens, form families, and seek Babylon’s welfare make sense alongside the warning against prophets who promise a quick return: the captivity is to be lived through as a long-term reality. The seventy years named in verse 10 is tied here to both Babylonian domination and the promised restoration, though this period was understood in different ways in later biblical and Second Temple writings.

sections.title: A Letter for a Long Exile

blocks.text: Jeremiah 29 belongs to a wider portion of the book that includes narratives and letters as well as prophetic speeches. The received book of Jeremiah brings together several literary forms—poetry, prose sermons, narratives, letters, headings, restoration collections, oracles concerning nations, and an appendix—within a long and disputed compositional history. This helps account for why this chapter reads as an actual letter sent between Jerusalem and the community in Babylon.
